title: Longitudinal dynamics of gene expression and metabolomics in an aging population cohort

verified.what_i_actually_checked: No data file exists to open. I fetched the MultiMuTHER results website (43 KB of HTML) and found it is a Shiny web application serving 18 summary-statistics tables (S2-S19) from the server with no download button, no table export extension and no static files (tried /data/, /session/download/, /table_s2.csv - all HTTP 404). I listed the GitHub repository (Julia-Elsayed-Moustafa/MultiMuTHER) via the GitHub API: 14 R scripts and a README, zero data tables; the matching Zenodo release (record 20591588, MIT licence) is a 35 KB code zip. GEO has no record (searched 'MultiMuTHER' and 'TwinsUK': only two unrelated methylation series). BioStudies/ArrayExpress search for 'MultiMuTHER' returned 0 hits. I listed all 20 datasets under the TwinsUK data access committee at the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGAC00001000274): every one is access_type 'controlled', and none is MultiMuTHER. The accepted author manuscript at King's College London (which includes the supplement) is blocked by a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403 on two attempts), as is the Science site and its supplementary zip.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All study numbers come from the abstract and the project website, not from files: 335 female participants, 3 or more visits over up to 8 years, 5,061 genes and 181 metabolites changing over time, whole-blood bulk RNA sequencing plus Metabolon serum metabolomics. I never read the paper's data availability statement itself - it is paywalled and the author manuscript download is blocked - so the access route is inferred from the TwinsUK data access portal, which requires a Data Access Proposal Form to the TwinsUK Resource Executive Committee (TREC), and from the fact that all TwinsUK depositions at the European Genome-phenome Archive are controlled.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL. Individual-level gene expression, metabolite and genotype data require a written application to the TwinsUK Resource Executive Committee plus a data sharing agreement; all 20 TwinsUK datasets at the European Genome-phenome Archive are marked 'controlled' and MultiMuTHER is not among them. The only open artifacts are analysis code (35 KB, no data) and a Shiny web app whose summary tables I verified have no bulk download route.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. For the obvious project (predict each person's molecular trajectory) the label would be a per-individual random slope the authors fitted, which is not a column in anything downloadable.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. No expression matrix or metabolite table is obtainable without an access application.

a4_units_stated.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. Website states expression and metabolite values were inverse-normal transformed, so units are rank-based, but no file was seen.

a5_enough_rows.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. Note the unit of analysis is the person: 335 individuals (paper text only), below the ~1,500-row guideline even if the data were open; roughly 1,000+ person-visit rows at best.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. A 335-person x ~20,000-gene matrix would be well under 1 GB, so size would not have been the problem.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. No file exists against which to check the 335 participants, 5,061 genes or 181 metabolites.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not assessed - stopped at A1. Flag for the record: the public summary statistics are effect sizes from the authors' own linear mixed-effects models, i.e. outputs of a fitted statistical model rather than raw measurements.

existing_models.name: Transcriptome-based aging clocks (blood RNA models that predict a person's age from gene expression) - e.g. the 'transcriptome-based aging clock near the theoretical limit of accuracy' preprint/paper and a 2025 Biogerontology blood-transcriptome age model
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported test-set correlations around 0.91-0.93 for gradient-boosted tree models on held-out individuals, per search-result summaries only; I retrieved titles and identifiers, not the full texts, so treat these numbers as unverified.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Search summaries state that clocks trained in one ethnic group fail to generalise to others; longitudinal within-person change over time is not what these cross-sectional clocks model.

backbone.name: Geneformer or scGPT (transformer models pretrained on large gene-expression corpora) would be the natural fit for blood expression profiles
backbone.hardware: Not assessed - no data to embed

integration.partner_dataset: GTEx (tissue gene expression) or the UK Biobank metabolomics panel, joinable in principle
integration.join_key: Ensembl gene identifier for genes; metabolite names or HMDB/KEGG identifiers for metabolites
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be pursued: the per-person longitudinal measurements that would make the join interesting are behind an access application, and the public summary statistics are gene-level effect sizes with no download route.

controls.positive_control: Would have been straightforward if data were open: a blood expression model must recover the textbook rise in inflammatory and loss of naive-T-cell signatures with age, and inferred sex from expression should be near-perfect.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle visit dates within each person and confirm all time effects vanish - not runnable without the data.
controls.external_validation: Other longitudinal blood cohorts exist in principle, but none was verified as openly downloadable here.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible from the public release: the only downloadable artifacts are 14 R analysis scripts and a web page, so any model would have to be trained on data obtained through a TwinsUK access application, after which the honest claim would be limited to 'predicts molecular change over up to 8 years among older British female twins who stayed enrolled for three or more visits'.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a person's blood gene activity and blood metabolite levels now to predict how both will change over the next few years.
plain_idea.train_on: Repeated whole-blood RNA sequencing (gene activity) plus serum metabolite measurements from the same women at three or more clinic visits spanning up to eight years. 335 participants, per the abstract; I verified no row count because no data file is obtainable.
plain_idea.predict: Each person's rate of change for each gene and metabolite - in the paper this is the per-individual slope from a mixed-effects model fitted to repeated measurements made by RNA sequencing and the Metabolon mass-spectrometry platform.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Aging-biomarker groups and precision-medicine clinics want to know whether a single visit predicts an individual's future molecular trajectory, since nearly every existing aging clock is built from one-time snapshots. Even a negative result would show that trajectories are not forecastable from baseline.

more_or_better_data.why: Repeated sampling of the same people three or more times over eight years is genuinely rarer than the single-visit cohorts behind published blood aging clocks, but at 335 people it is far smaller than those training sets (hundreds to over a thousand donors), and none of it is accessible.

confidence_score.why: Three or more visits per person plus monozygotic twin pairs would in principle let you separate measurement noise from real within-person change, which snapshot clocks cannot do - but I could not confirm replicate structure in any file.

models_beatable.why: Published blood transcriptome age models already use modern gradient-boosted trees and report around 0.91-0.93 correlation on held-out individuals, and in any case the comparison cannot be run because this paper's data is not obtainable.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: we cannot obtain the data, so no baseline can be run on it and no model can see it.

ml_idea: Predict each individual's multi-year molecular trajectory (per-gene and per-metabolite rate of change) from a single baseline visit, with twin pairs used to separate heritable from environmental components of trajectory. The idea is sound but unexecutable: the individual-level data requires a TwinsUK access application, and the public release is summary statistics in a web app with no download.

effort.compute_note: No estimates possible - no data file was obtainable, so nothing was loaded or timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Check whether any individual-level file can be downloaded without an application. Done in under thirty minutes: the TwinsUK portal requires a Data Access Proposal Form to its Resource Executive Committee, all 20 TwinsUK depositions at the European Genome-phenome Archive are marked controlled, GEO and ArrayExpress have nothing, and the public website's tables have no download endpoint.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails. The individual-level longitudinal gene expression and metabolite data belongs to the TwinsUK cohort and requires a written application to its Resource Executive Committee plus a data sharing agreement; I confirmed GEO, ArrayExpress and the European Genome-phenome Archive hold no open deposition (all 20 TwinsUK EGA datasets are 'controlled'). The only openly available artifacts are 14 R analysis scripts on GitHub/Zenodo (35 KB, no data) and a Shiny web application of gene-level summary statistics that I verified has no download button and no static file endpoints. Even setting access aside, the unit of analysis is 335 people, below the row guideline, and the public numbers are effect sizes from the authors' own mixed-effects models rather than raw measurements.
